why: NaOH turns red litmus blue and dissolves readily, while its dissolution is exothermic (beaker warm, not cold) and a base cannot turn blue litmus red.
solution: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, so it turns red litmus blue and observation (1) is correct, and it is highly soluble in water, so observation (2) is correct. Observation (4) directly contradicts (1), since a base can never turn blue litmus red, and observation (3) is wrong because dissolving \(\text{NaOH}\) in water is strongly exothermic, so the outside of the beaker feels warm rather than cold. Only (1) and (2) survive. Matches option A.

why: Ionic bond holds cations and anions, catenation is carbon self-linking, pyridine is a denaturant for alcohol, and synthetic detergents are non-biodegradable.
solution: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction that holds cations and anions together, so (i) pairs with (a). The self-linking of carbon atoms into long chains and rings is catenation, so (ii) pairs with (c), and denatured alcohol is ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding substances such as pyridine or methanol, so (iii) pairs with (b). Synthetic detergents carry branched hydrocarbon chains that micro-organisms cannot break down, so (iv) pairs with (d). Matches option D.

why: Buckminsterfullerene is the sixty-carbon cage molecule, an allotrope of carbon alongside diamond and graphite.
solution: Buckminsterfullerene, \(\text{C}_{60}\), is a cage-like molecule of sixty carbon atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons like a football. It is therefore an allotropic form of carbon, taking its place beside diamond and graphite. Matches option D.

why: Ethyl propanoate and methyl butanoate are both \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2\) with ten hydrogens, while propyl methanoate has eight and ethyl butanoate twelve.
solution: Ethyl propanoate is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5\), that is \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2\), which carries ten hydrogen atoms, and methyl butanoate is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3\), also \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2\). Propyl methanoate is \(\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\), i.e. \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2\) with only eight hydrogens, and ethyl butanoate is \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2\) with twelve. So esters (i) and (iii) alone qualify. Matches option C.

why: Ethyne has one triple bond (six shared electrons) plus two C-H bonds (four more), giving ten shared electrons in all.
solution: Ethyne is \(\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}\). The carbon-carbon triple bond is three shared pairs, that is six electrons, and each of the two carbon-hydrogen bonds contributes one shared pair, adding four more. The total number of electrons shared in the molecule is therefore \(6 + 4 = 10\). Matches option A.

why: Identical atoms have identical electronegativity, so the bonding pair is shared equally in a non-polar covalent bond.
solution: Two identical non-metal atoms have exactly the same electronegativity, so neither can pull the shared pair towards itself. The bonding electron pair therefore lies symmetrically between the two nuclei, giving a non-polar covalent bond as in \(\text{H}_2\) or \(\text{Cl}_2\). Complete transfer would produce an ionic bond, which cannot happen between two identical atoms. Matches option D.

why: Only propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate are actually \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\); the aldehyde and ketone offered elsewhere are \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}\).
solution: The formula \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\) demands two oxygen atoms, which immediately rules out options A, B and C, because \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3\) are both \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}\) with a single oxygen. Propanoic acid, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\), and methyl ethanoate, \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3\), each contain three carbons, six hydrogens and two oxygens, so they are the required pair of isomers bearing the carboxylic acid and the ester group. Matches option D.

why: The scattering experiment established the dense positive nucleus and the emptiness of the atom; the electron's charge and the neutron came from other work.
solution: The few \(\alpha\) particles that were turned back through large angles showed that the whole of the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, and the overwhelming majority passing straight through undeflected showed that most of the atom is empty space, so statements (2) and (4) are conclusions of the experiment. The negative charge on the electron had already been established by Thomson using discharge tubes, and the neutron was discovered much later by Chadwick, so (1) and (3) are not. Matches option B.

why: Isobars are different elements so their chemistry differs (true), but protons plus neutrons is the mass number, which for isobars is the same, not different (false).
solution: Isobars are atoms of different elements that happen to have the same mass number but different atomic numbers, so their electron arrangements differ and their chemical properties differ; statement 1 is true. The sum of protons and neutrons is precisely the mass number, and for isobars that sum is identical rather than different, so statement 2 is false as written. Matches option A.

why: ABSTAIN: the answer is carried entirely by the diagram, which I cannot see, and three of the four options name genuinely different models.
solution: The figure alone decides this question. Thomson's model is drawn as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon, Rutherford's shows a dense central nucleus with electrons revolving around it in open space, and Bohr's shows electrons confined to discrete concentric shells of fixed energy. Chadwick proposed no model of the atom at all, only the neutron, so that option can be eliminated on principle, but the remaining three cannot be separated without sight of the diagram.

why: Carbon has four valence electrons not six, and the two \(A=40\) atoms are isobars not isotopes; the valency rule and the C-14/N-15/O-16 isotone set are both correct.
solution: Carbon has the configuration 2,4 and therefore four valence electrons, not six, so statement 1 is false, and \(^{40}_{18}X\) and \(^{40}_{20}Y\) share a mass number but not an atomic number, which makes them isobars rather than isotopes, so statement 2 is false. Statement 3 is the standard rule linking valency to the outermost shell, and in statement 4 the neutron counts are \(14-6=8\), \(15-7=8\) and \(16-8=8\), so all three nuclides do have eight neutrons and are isotones. Only (3) and (4) are correct. Matches option A.

why: Thomson found the same \(e/m\) whatever gas or electrode material was used, which is what proved the electron universal.
solution: When Thomson measured the charge to mass ratio of the cathode-ray particles he obtained the same value, about \(1.76\times10^{11}\) C/kg, no matter which gas filled the discharge tube and no matter which metal the electrodes were made of. That invariance is exactly what showed the electron to be a fundamental particle present in the atoms of every element. Matches option C.

why: A diprotic acid and a diacidic base at equal volume and equal concentration neutralise exactly, leaving a neutral solution, which universal indicator shows green.
solution: Sulphuric acid supplies two \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions per molecule and magnesium hydroxide supplies two \(\text{OH}^{-}\) ions per formula unit, so equal volumes of equal concentration contain equal numbers of each and they cancel exactly: \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Mg(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\). The resulting solution is neutral at \(\text{pH}\) 7, and universal indicator is green at that value. Matches option C.

why: Sodium hydrogencarbonate is a weak base of \(\text{pH}\) about 8 and is safe on skin, hence mild and non-corrosive.
solution: Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, \(\text{NaHCO}_3\), the salt of the strong base \(\text{NaOH}\) and the weak acid \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\), so its solution is only weakly basic with a \(\text{pH}\) of roughly 8. Because the base is weak it does not attack skin or tissue the way sodium hydroxide does, which is precisely why it can be used in cooking and as an antacid. Matches option A.

why: A normal salt has no replaceable \(\text{H}^{+}\) or \(\text{OH}^{-}\) left, and from a strong acid and strong base it hydrolyses in neither direction, so it is neutral.
solution: A normal salt is one in which every replaceable hydrogen of the parent acid has been replaced by a metal, so the salt itself carries no ionisable \(\text{H}^{+}\) and no \(\text{OH}^{-}\). When the parent acid and base are both strong, as in \(\text{NaCl}\) from \(\text{HCl}\) and \(\text{NaOH}\), neither ion hydrolyses in water and the solution stays neutral at \(\text{pH}\) 7. Matches option D.

why: Only red litmus gives a visible difference: it turns blue in NaOH and is unchanged in water, whereas blue litmus, dilute HCl and sodium carbonate give no visible signal in either tube.
solution: Sodium hydroxide is a base, so red litmus dipped into it turns blue while the same paper dipped in water stays red, giving an unmistakable difference between the two tubes. Blue litmus remains blue in both, and neither dilute hydrochloric acid nor sodium carbonate solution produces any visible change with water or with sodium hydroxide, so none of those three can identify the tube. Matches option B.

why: Plaster of Paris, the hemihydrate, sets to a hard mass on adding water and is the material used to seal joints airtight.
solution: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, \(\text{CaSO}_4\cdot\frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}\). On mixing with water it takes up the remaining water of crystallisation and sets rapidly into a hard solid mass, expanding very slightly as it does so, which is what lets it fill and seal gaps in an apparatus and make the assembly airtight. Gypsum, white vitriol and Epsom salt are already fully hydrated and show no such setting action. Matches option D.

why: Adding 273 gives 308 K, 329 K and 391 K; the rival option miscomputes the last value as 392 K.
solution: A Celsius temperature is converted using \(T(\text{K}) = t(^\circ\text{C}) + 273\). This gives \(35 + 273 = 308\), \(56 + 273 = 329\) and \(118 + 273 = 391\), so the three boiling points are 308 K, 329 K and 391 K. The nearest rival option reproduces the first two correctly but gives 392 K for n-butyl alcohol, which is one kelvin too high. Matches option A.

why: An ice-and-water mixture sits at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) and holds there while latent heat of fusion is absorbed, then rises, which is graph IV.
solution: The beaker begins with ice and water together, so its contents are at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). All the heat supplied at first is spent as latent heat of fusion melting the ice, so the thermometer holds steady at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) even though heating continues, and only once the last of the ice has melted does the water start to warm towards \(100^\circ\text{C}\). Graph IV is the one that shows a plateau at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) followed by a rise. Matches option B.

why: Water boils at \(100^\circ\text{C}\); note the option set is defective because \(212^\circ\text{F}\) is the same temperature and is equally true.
solution: At one atmosphere pressure water boils at \(100^\circ\text{C}\), which is 373 K on the Kelvin scale, while \(0^\circ\text{C}\) is the melting point of ice. Note that \(212^\circ\text{F}\) is exactly the same temperature expressed on the Fahrenheit scale, since \(t(^\circ\text{F}) = \frac{9}{5}(100) + 32 = 212\), so that option is equally true and the question as printed has two correct answers; the Celsius value is the one the textbook convention intends. Matches option B.

why: Dry ice is stored under pressure and sublimes when the pressure falls to one atmosphere, and warming also drives it, so both factors act; a single-factor option would leave two options true.
solution: Solid carbon dioxide is stored under high pressure, and when the pressure is released to one atmosphere it passes straight from solid to gas without ever melting, so a fall in pressure drives the change of state. Raising the temperature drives it as well, because at one atmosphere dry ice sublimes as soon as its surroundings are warmer than about \(-78^\circ\text{C}\), which is why a block of it steadily disappears in an open room. Since each factor on its own would make a separate option true, the combined statement is the only self-consistent answer. Matches option D.

why: The kelvin is written without a degree symbol, and mercury is chosen because it does not wet glass; both statements are true.
solution: On the Kelvin scale the unit is written simply as K, for example 273 K, because the kelvin is an absolute unit and by convention takes no degree symbol, so statement A is true. Mercury is used in glass thermometers because it does not wet or stick to the glass, so the thread runs freely and breaks cleanly to give an accurate reading, and it is opaque and expands uniformly besides, so statement B is true as well. Matches option D.

why: Heat is liberated so the reaction is exothermic, and the product calcium hydroxide is a base, so the \(\text{pH}\) exceeds 7.
solution: The reaction is \(\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2\), and because heat is given out to the surroundings it is exothermic by definition. Calcium hydroxide is a base and its solution, lime water, contains \(\text{OH}^{-}\) ions, so the \(\text{pH}\) of the solution formed is greater than 7. Matches option A.

why: Sulphur dioxide has the burning-sulphur smell, turns lime water milky and reduces acidified dichromate from orange to green.
solution: Heating ferrous sulphate crystals decomposes them: \(2\text{FeSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{SO}_3\). Sulphur dioxide is colourless with the choking smell of burning sulphur, it turns lime water milky by forming calcium sulphite, and being a reducing agent it turns orange acidified potassium dichromate green by reducing chromium from the plus six to the plus three state. Carbon dioxide fails the smell and dichromate tests, hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs, and nitrogen dioxide is brown. Matches option C.

why: Displaced copper deposits as loosely packed particles rather than a plated layer, so the coating is rough and granular.
solution: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it from the solution: \(\text{Fe} + \text{CuSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4 + \text{Cu}\). The copper comes out of solution quickly and settles on the nail as loosely packed particles rather than as an even electroplated film, so the reddish-brown deposit that a student sees and can rub off is rough and granular rather than smooth, shiny or flaky. Matches option B.

why: Only calcium displacing copper and magnesium displacing zinc run, since each displacing metal must be the more reactive one.
solution: A metal displaces another from its salt solution only when it stands higher in the activity series. Calcium lies well above copper, so case 2 gives \(\text{CuSO}_4 + \text{Ca} \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 + \text{Cu}\), and magnesium lies above zinc, so case 4 gives \(\text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4 + \text{Zn}\). Aluminium and copper both lie below calcium, so cases 1 and 3 produce nothing. Matches option A.

why: Quick lime with water gives slaked lime, a metal hydroxide releasing \(\text{OH}^{-}\), hence basic.
solution: Quick lime is calcium oxide, and its action with water produces slaked lime: \(\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2\). Calcium hydroxide is the hydroxide of a metal and furnishes \(\text{OH}^{-}\) ions in solution, turning red litmus blue, so the new product is basic in nature. Matches option D.

why: Thirteen protons identifies aluminium: configuration 2,8,3 gives valency three and \(\text{AlCl}_3\), and \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) is amphoteric, so all three statements hold.
solution: An element with thirteen protons has atomic number 13 and is aluminium, whose electronic configuration is 2,8,3. Three valence electrons give it a valency of three, so its chloride is \(\text{AlCl}_3\), and its oxide \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) dissolves in acids to give aluminium salts and in alkalis to give aluminates, which is exactly what makes it amphoteric. All three statements are therefore correct. Matches option C.

why: Softness, instant tarnishing and a violent reaction with cold water identify sodium, which is stored under kerosene for that reason.
solution: Sodium is soft enough to be cut with a knife, tarnishes the instant a fresh surface is exposed to air, and reacts with cold water so vigorously that the hydrogen released catches fire: \(2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\). It is for this reason that sodium is kept immersed in kerosene. Magnesium reacts only with hot water, calcium reacts far more gently and is not stored under kerosene, and phosphorus is a non-metal. Matches option A.

why: Being beaten into sheets is malleability, a metallic property, and zinc is the only metal listed.
solution: The ability to be beaten into thin sheets is malleability, and it is a characteristic property of metals because their layers of atoms can slide over one another without the metallic bonding breaking. Zinc is the only metal among the four choices, while oxygen is a gas and sulphur and phosphorus are solid non-metals that are brittle and crumble to powder when hammered. Matches option A.

why: In the series K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, magnesium indeed lies below calcium and above aluminium; the other three statements invert real positions.
solution: Reading the activity series downwards the order is potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, mercury, silver and gold. Magnesium sits immediately below calcium and immediately above aluminium, so that statement agrees with the series. Copper is below lead rather than above it, iron is above lead and not below it, and zinc lies below aluminium and not above it, so the other three statements are all false. Matches option D.

why: KCl and NaCl are metal-plus-non-metal ionic solids, while HCl and \(\text{CCl}_4\) are made only of non-metals and are covalent.
solution: An ionic compound is formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal, which is the case for potassium chloride and sodium chloride. Hydrogen chloride and carbon tetrachloride contain no metal at all and are held together by shared electron pairs, so they are covalent, which is why \(\text{CCl}_4\) does not conduct electricity in any state and pure \(\text{HCl}\) conducts only after its molecules ionise in water. The two that are not ionic are therefore (2) and (3). Matches option A.

why: Being drawn into wire is ductility, distinct from malleability, conductivity and sonorousity.
solution: Ductility is the property that allows a metal to be drawn out into thin wire, which is why copper and aluminium are used for electrical cables. Malleability is the different property of being hammered into sheets, conductivity is the ability to carry heat or electric current, and sonorousity is the ability to produce a ringing sound when struck. Matches option C.

why: Conduction in the solid state means a metal (Pb); never conducting means a covalent non-metal (S); conducting only in water means covalent HCl; conducting when molten or aqueous means ionic NaCl.
solution: A substance that conducts in the molten state and also as a solid must have mobile free electrons, so Y is the metal lead, and a substance that conducts under no condition at all must be a covalent non-metal, so W is sulphur. Hydrogen chloride is covalent and conducts only once its molecules ionise on dissolving, so X is \(\text{HCl}\), while sodium chloride is ionic and conducts as soon as its ions are free to move, that is when melted or dissolved but not while solid, so Z is \(\text{NaCl}\). Matches option D.
